description: We are young and full of dreams
summary: SOL 500 is a free survival and base-building game that teaches space science to students aged 9-15 and to 18. Players run an outpost on Mars and try to keep their crew alive for 500 sols. They pack the lander, give each astronaut a job, build solar panels, greenhouses and radiation shields, and explore an endless map of Mars on foot, by rover and by drone. Along the way they live through dust storms, solar flares and oxygen cuts. The game's numbers come from cited NASA sources, and its physics engine uses Newton's laws with Mars gravity. While the rover drives, two lines on the ground, "Earth stop" and "Mars stop", show that it needs 2.6 times as far to brake on Mars. The ground is made from real NASA photos, and the game has a Science Notes page and links to NASA and CSA learning tools. Up to five players can play together, and it works offline in English and Vietnamese
details:
What it does:

SOL 500 is a survival and base-building game for students aged 15–18. Your job is to keep a crew alive on Mars for 500 sols (Mars days). You pack the lander and give each astronaut a job: Scientist, Engineer, Biologist or Medic. Then you build the outpost (solar panels, greenhouses, water extractors, radiation shields, life support) and grow it from a Camp to a Colony. You walk your astronaut and drive rovers and a scout drone across an endless map of Mars with six kinds of land, from the Dune Sea to the Icy Plains. Dust storms, solar flares, water leaks, late supply ships and oxygen cuts make you decide fast: take shelter, ration, or go out and find more oxygen.

How it works:

The game's numbers come from cited NASA sources. A small physics engine uses Newton's laws with Mars gravity (3.73 m/s², 38% of Earth's), so a rover needs about 2.6 times as far to stop as it would on Earth. Two dashed lines in front of the rover, "Earth stop" and "Mars stop", show the difference while you drive. The ground uses real NASA photos and landmarks come with NASA facts. The game also has a Science Notes page, a field guide and a Resources page that links to NASA and CSA learning tools. Up to 5 players can play together on the same Wi-Fi, or from anywhere with a share link.

Benefits and intended impact:

Students learn physics and space science by using it to survive, not by memorising it. The debrief at the end of each mission explains what happened and teaches ISRU, which means living off Martian resources. The game is free and open source, plays offline in any modern browser, needs no account, and comes in English and Vietnamese so Vietnamese students can learn real space science in their own language. Teachers can host co-op games for a class and see game history in the admin panel. The goal is to get more teenagers, especially in Vietnam, interested in STEM and space careers.

Tools, languages, hardware and software:

- JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG and HTML Canvas, with no game engine or framework

- Node.js server with WebSockets for co-op, QR codes for the join link, and a Cloudflare tunnel for the online share link

- Electron and electron-builder for the Windows app and installer; it also works as an installable web app and as a single HTML file that runs offline

- Node's built-in test runner, with 906 automated tests

- Git and GitHub for version control and releases (390 commits, now version 3.9.2, MIT license)

- Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help write, test and review the code

- Chatgpt, to help adjust layout and content of the demo slide

- NASA data and images; built on a Windows laptop and tested in Chrome

How it is creative

- It shows the physics instead of explaining it: the Earth stop and Mars stop lines make gravity something you can see.

- The fictional "Kestrel Survey" robots landed before your crew and left weather stations and supply caches to find, so exploring keeps surprising you.

- In the Showcase gallery, each card opens the real game at that exact moment (rover physics, a solar flare, base ranks), which works well for classroom demos.

- A short launch and landing film, drawn in the game's own art style, plays when the crew leaves Earth and comes home.

- In co-op, each player controls one astronaut, so crew roles and teamwork matter.

Factors we considered

- Audience: short, clear sentences for ages 15–18, a How to Play guide with 12 picture cards, and Training and Quick modes for beginners.

- Scientific accuracy: every fact names its NASA source, and I removed claims I couldn't back up.

- Access: free, works offline, no account, two languages, and it respects the computer's reduced-motion setting.

- Safety and privacy: no personal data is collected, the admin panel needs a password and can't be reached through the share link, and there are no API keys in the code.

- Balance: I tuned the difficulty with hundreds of simulated games played by computer players, so the game is hard but fair.

- Reliability: all 906 tests run and the installer is checked on a real PC before every release.
dataRefs: 1/Radiation budget The cruise to Mars and back adds about 660 mSv (1.84 mSv per day for 360 days). NASA’s career limit is 600 mSv, so a real crew is already over it before landing. That is an unsolved problem. The game gives each astronaut a 300 mSv surface budget to make the trade-off visible.
https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/radiation-protection-technical-brief-ochmo.pdf

Oxygen, water and food NASA’s life-support baseline is about 0.84 kg of oxygen per person per day. Drinking and food water is about 3.5 kg, roughly doubled by hygiene. Packaged ISS food runs about 1.8 kg per person per day with packaging.
https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20180001338
Recycling water The ISS now recovers 98 % of its water from humidity and urine. The game uses 93 %, a little below the best result, because Mars dust and gravity add risk.
https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/nasa-achieves-water-recovery-milestone-on-international-space-station/
Oxygen from the air MOXIE on Perseverance pulled oxygen out of Martian CO₂ 16 times, making 122 g in total and up to 12 g per hour. The game’s O₂ plant is a scaled-up MOXIE.
https://www.nasa.gov/missions/mars-2020-perseverance/perseverance-rover/nasas-oxygen-generating-experiment-moxie-completes-mars-mission/
Nuclear power NASA’s Kilopower test in 2018 ran a reactor designed to give 1 to 10 kW for at least 10 years.
https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/kilopower-media-event-charts-final-011618.pdf
The Fission Surface Power project is now aiming for 40 kW for the Moon and later Mars.
https://www.nasa.gov/exploration-systems-development-mission-directorate/fission-surface-power/

Dust storms In June 2018 a planet-wide dust storm blocked sunlight over Opportunity for months. Its solar-powered batteries ran down and the rover never woke up. In the game a global storm cuts solar output to about 8 %.
https://science.nasa.gov/missions/mer/nasas-opportunity-rover-mission-on-mars-comes-to-end/

Dust devils Solar panels on Spirit and Opportunity slowly gathered dust, but passing whirlwinds sometimes blew them clean and boosted power. The game models dust as a slow loss that maintenance and dust devils undo.
https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/spirit-gets-energy-boost-from-cleaner-solar-panels/
Perchlorate The Phoenix lander found perchlorate salts, about 0.5 % of the soil by weight. They are toxic to people and must be washed out before soil is used for growing food.
https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20190028297
Solar conjunction About every two years the Sun sits between Earth and Mars. NASA stops sending commands for about two weeks because the Sun’s plasma can corrupt radio signals.
https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/whats-mars-solar-conjunction-and-why-does-it-matter/
Fresh food Astronauts grow lettuce and other crops in the ISS Veggie chamber. Studies show that tending plants and eating fresh food help crew morale.
https://www.nasa.gov/exploration-research-and-technology/growing-plants-in-space/

Designer plants NASA reported in 2013 that its Institute for Advanced Concepts was funding scientists at North Carolina State University to design plants for a greenhouse on Mars. There they would face strong ultraviolet light by day, temperatures well below freezing at night and soil poor in nutrients. As a first step, the team put a gene from Pyrococcus furiosus, a microbe from the scalding water of deep-sea vents, into tobacco cells, and it worked without harming them. Such plants could give astronauts oxygen, fresh food and even medicine.
https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-designer-plants-on-mars/

Mission length NASA’s Design Reference Architecture 5.0 plans a conjunction-class mission with about 500 days on the surface while Earth and Mars line up again for the trip home. Cargo landers go ahead of the crew, which inspired the orbital supply drops.
https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20090040343

projectRefs: Radiation on the surface Curiosity’s RAD instrument measured about 0.64 mSv per sol at Gale Crater. Mars has no global magnetic field and a thin atmosphere, so cosmic rays reach the ground. SOL 500 uses that rate, reduced by your shielding.

2/Radiation budget The cruise to Mars and back adds about 660 mSv (1.84 mSv per day for 360 days). NASA’s career limit is 600 mSv, so a real crew is already over it before landing. That is an unsolved problem. The game gives each astronaut a 300 mSv surface budget to make the trade-off visible.
